title: Introduction to R
text:
What is R?
R is a free, open-source programming language and computing environment built for statistics and data analysis. It is widely used across psychology, education, public health, and the social sciences — and it is what we will use throughout this course.
Unlike point-and-click software such as SPSS, R is a scripting language. You write a sequence of instructions, and R executes them in order. This takes practice at first, but the payoff is significant: your analyses are reproducible, shareable, and easy to modify.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Why Use R?

Free. R costs nothing and runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
Reproducible. Your entire analysis lives in a script you can re-run, share, or hand to a reviewer.
Powerful and flexible. From t-tests to multilevel models to machine learning — R handles it all.
Standard in research. R is the dominant tool in academic psychology and education research. Learning it now is an investment you will use throughout your career.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Installing R and RStudio
You need two things. Install them in order.

1. R — the language itself

Download from cran.r-project.org. Choose your operating system and install the current release.

2. RStudio — the editor that makes R easier to use

Download the free RStudio Desktop from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop. Always open RStudio, not R directly.


Think of R as the engine and RStudio as the dashboard.

The RStudio Interface
When RStudio opens you will see four panes:







Pane
Purpose




Source (top-left)
Write and save your scripts here


Console (bottom-left)
Where R runs code and shows output


Environment (top-right)
Objects currently stored in memory


Files / Plots / Help (bottom-right)
Browse files, view plots, read documentation



Write your code in the Source pane and run it with Ctrl+Enter (Windows) or Cmd+Return (Mac). Results appear in the Console.

title: Introduction to R
text:
R as a Calculator
The simplest thing R can do is arithmetic. Type any expression and press Enter:
1 + 1
[1] 2
The [1] at the start of every output line just means “first element of the result.” You will see it everywhere.
10 - 3        # subtraction
4 * 5         # multiplication
20 / 4        # division
2 ^ 8         # exponentiation  →  256
sqrt(144)     # square root     →  12
abs(-7)       # absolute value  →  7






TipThe # symbol marks a comment



Everything after # on a line is a comment — R ignores it when running the code. Use comments freely to explain what each line does. Your future self will thank you.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Objects
In R, you can store any value in a named object using the assignment arrow <-:
X <- 8
Now X holds the value 8. Call it by name to see it:
X
[1] 8
You can use objects in calculations just like raw numbers:
X + 2       # 10
X * X       # 64
sqrt(X)     # 2.828427
Object names are case-sensitive: X and x are two different objects.

Vectors
A vector is a sequence of values stored together. Create one with c() — short for “combine”:
Y <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Y
[1] 1 2 3 4 5
Operations on a vector apply to every element at once:
Y + 10       # [1] 11 12 13 14 15
Y * 2        # [1]  2  4  6  8 10
Vectors can also hold text (called character strings):
names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol")
names
[1] "Alice" "Bob"   "Carol"


Matrices
A matrix is a two-dimensional table of values — rows and columns. Create one with matrix():
Z <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
Z
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    4    7
[2,]    2    5    8
[3,]    3    6    9
Values fill in column by column by default. You can transpose with t(Z).

title: Introduction to R
text:
Classes
Every object in R has a class — a label that tells R what kind of thing it is and which operations are valid. You can check it with class():
class(8)            # "numeric"
class("hello")      # "character"
class(TRUE)         # "logical"
class(c(1,2,3))     # "numeric"






NoteWhy classes matter



Almost every error in R comes down to a class mismatch — trying to do math on a character vector, or passing a data frame to a function that expects a single number. Checking the class of your objects is the first debugging step.

title: Introduction to R
text:
A First Look at Data
Real datasets in R are stored as data frames — tables with rows (observations) and columns (variables). R ships with several built-in datasets for practice.
mtcars has data on 32 cars:
head(mtcars)       # first 6 rows
Use $ to pull out a single column by name:
mtcars$cyl         # cylinder counts for all 32 cars
 [1] 6 6 4 6 8 6 8 4 4 6 6 8 8 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 4 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 8 6 8 4
A few useful inspection functions:
dim(mtcars)        # rows, columns:  32  11
names(mtcars)      # variable names
class(mtcars)      # "data.frame"
class(mtcars$mpg)  # "numeric"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Getting Help
When you are unsure how a function works, prefix it with ?:
?mean
?sqrt
?matrix
The Help pane opens with the function’s documentation: description, arguments, and worked examples. ??keyword searches all installed documentation.

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
text: We continue working with readtime.csv, but now we add a second independent variable. In addition to Device (Phone, Tablet, Laptop), participants read under different lighting conditions (Blue, White, Yellow, Natural). Each participant was assigned to exactly one device type and one lighting condition, making this a 3 × 4 between-subjects factorial design (12 groups, 5 participants per group, N = 60).

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Packages
# install.packages("psych")
# install.packages("emmeans")
# install.packages("effectsize")

library(psych)
library(emmeans)
library(effectsize)

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Load and Prepare the Data
reader <- read.csv("readtime.csv")

Recoding factor levels
The variables Device and Light are stored as numbers. We need to tell R they are categorical and give them meaningful labels. The cleanest way is with factor(), which sets levels and labels in a single line — no extra packages needed.
reader$Device <- factor(reader$Device,
                        levels = 1:3,
                        labels = c("Phone", "Tablet", "Laptop"))

reader$Light  <- factor(reader$Light,
                        levels = 1:4,
                        labels = c("Blue", "White", "Yellow", "Natural"))

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Visualizing the Interaction
Before fitting the model, plot the cell means. If the lines are roughly parallel, it suggests no interaction — the effect of one factor is the same regardless of the level of the other.

Quick check: interaction.plot()
interaction.plot() is a base R function that requires no additional packages and is useful for a quick look at your data during analysis.
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 8))   # widen right margin so the legend is not cut off

interaction.plot(
  x.factor     = reader$Light,
  trace.factor = reader$Device,
  response     = reader$ReadingTime,
  fun          = mean,
  xlab         = "Lighting Condition",
  ylab         = "Mean Reading Time (ms)",
  trace.label  = "Device",
  col          = c("steelblue", "darkorchid", "tomato"),
  lwd          = 2
)

par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))   # reset margins to default






Note



Limitation of interaction.plot()
Because this is a base R function, the legend is drawn outside the plot region and its placement depends on your window size — the device names can be cut off if the plot is too narrow. The overall appearance is also not publication-ready. Use interaction.plot() to get a fast visual check during your analysis, then switch to the ggplot2 version below when you need a clean figure for a paper or presentation.




Publication-ready plot: ggplot2
# install.packages("ggplot2")   # run once if needed
# install.packages("dplyr")

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

reader %>%
  group_by(Device, Light) %>%
  summarise(mean_RT = mean(ReadingTime), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Light, y = mean_RT, color = Device, group = Device)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    x     = "Lighting Condition",
    y     = "Mean Reading Time (ms)",
    color = "Device"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot2 reads the factor levels directly, so the legend will correctly label each line “Phone”, “Tablet”, and “Laptop” regardless of window size. The plot can be exported at any resolution with ggsave().
The three lines track closely together and run roughly parallel across all four lighting conditions — a visual cue that Device and Light are acting independently rather than interacting.

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Fitting the Model
The * operator fits both main effects and their interaction in one step.
fit2.way <- aov(ReadingTime ~ Device * Light, data = reader)
summary(fit2.way)
             Df  Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)
Device        2  706968  353484   4.648  0.01428 *
Light         3 1481064  493688   6.492  0.00089 ***
Device:Light  6   21543    3591   0.047  0.99953
Residuals    48 3650203   76046






Note



Reading the factorial ANOVA table
There are three tests:

Device main effect: Does reading time differ by device type, averaging across all lighting conditions? F(2, 48) = 4.65, p = .014 — yes.
Light main effect: Does reading time differ by lighting condition, averaging across all devices? F(3, 48) = 6.49, p < .001 — yes.
Device × Light interaction: Does the effect of device change depending on which light is used (or vice versa)? F(6, 48) = 0.047, p = .9995 — no.

The near-zero F for the interaction (0.047) with a p-value of .9995 tells us the two factors act completely independently. The advantage of phones over tablets is essentially the same under blue light, white light, yellow light, and natural light. This is what statisticians call an additive relationship.

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Overall Effect Sizes: Eta Squared
Eta squared (η²) is the proportion of total variance in reading time explained by each effect.
eta_squared(fit2.way, partial = FALSE)
# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)

Parameter    |  Eta2 |       95% CI
------------------------------------
Device       |  0.12 | [0.00, 1.00]
Light        |  0.25 | [0.07, 1.00]
Device:Light |  0.004| [0.00, 1.00]

Device: η² = .12 — device type explains 12% of the total variance in reading time.
Light: η² = .25 — lighting condition explains 25% of the total variance. This is the stronger of the two main effects.
Interaction: η² < .01 — the Device × Light combination explains essentially none of the variance.







Note



η² vs. partial η²
In a one-way ANOVA, η² and partial η² are identical. In a factorial design they differ: partial η² estimates each effect’s share of variance after removing the other effects, which inflates the values (e.g., Device partial η² = .16 vs. full η² = .12). Full η² is more conservative and directly interpretable as a proportion of total variance. Partial η² is commonly reported in published articles when comparing across studies with different designs.

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
section: When the Interaction Is Not Significant
text:
When the Interaction Is Not Significant






Tip



The interaction guides your next step
In a factorial ANOVA, always look at the interaction first:

If the interaction IS significant: the main effects are misleading on their own. You must decompose the interaction using simple effects — for example, testing Device differences separately within each level of Light. The main effect averages across conditions that behave differently, which obscures what is really happening.
If the interaction is NOT significant (as here): the two factors act independently and additively. It is safe — and correct — to interpret the main effects directly. The effect of Device is the same across all lighting levels, so averaging across them gives an accurate picture.

Because our interaction is not significant, we proceed to main-effect post-hoc tests for Device and Light separately.

title: Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
section: If the Interaction Had Been Significant: Simple Effects
text:
If the Interaction Had Been Significant: Simple Effects
When an interaction is significant, interpreting the main effects alone is misleading — the effect of Device depends on which lighting level you are in, so averaging across lighting levels obscures what is actually happening. This is the cost of decomposing an interaction — you gain specificity (knowing where the effect occurs) but lose precision.

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text: The dataset for this week is mind.csv. Ten participants had their blood pressure (BP) measured at four time points: Before an intervention, at One Month, Three Months, and Six Months post-intervention. Because the same participants were measured at every time point, this is a within-subjects (repeated measures) design.

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text:
Packages
# install.packages("reshape2")    # run once if needed
# install.packages("psych")
# install.packages("emmeans")
# install.packages("effectsize")

library(reshape2)
library(psych)
library(emmeans)
library(effectsize)

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text:
Load and Prepare the Data

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text:
Checking Assumptions
The key normality assumption for repeated measures ANOVA is that the difference scores between pairs of time points are normally distributed — not the raw scores themselves.
# Compute difference scores relative to baseline
d_1mo  <- mind$Before - mind$OneMonth
d_3mo  <- mind$Before - mind$ThreeMonth
d_6mo  <- mind$Before - mind$SixMonth

shapiro.test(d_1mo)
shapiro.test(d_3mo)
shapiro.test(d_6mo)
Before - OneMonth:    W = 0.94264, p-value = 0.5827
Before - ThreeMonth:  W = 0.93256, p-value = 0.4735
Before - SixMonth:    W = 0.96621, p-value = 0.8537
All three tests are non-significant, so there is no evidence against normality of the difference scores.






Note



Sphericity
Repeated measures ANOVA also assumes sphericity — that the variances of all pairwise difference scores are equal. This is tested with Mauchly’s test. If sphericity is violated, apply a Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt correction (both are available in SPSS; in R, the ez package provides them). For this small dataset we proceed with the standard model.

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text:
Visualizing Residuals
These plots help check the independence and constant-variance assumptions visually. Run them and look for random scatter (no patterns or fans).
fit_check <- lm(BP ~ Time, data = mind.melt)
N <- length(fit_check$residuals)

# Independence: residuals in observation order
plot(1:N, fit_check$residuals,
     xlab = "Observation order", ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Residuals vs. Order")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Homoscedasticity: residuals vs. fitted values
plot(fit_check$fitted.values, fit_check$residuals,
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs. Fitted")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Normality: Q-Q plot
qqnorm(fit_check$residuals, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot")
qqline(fit_check$residuals)

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text:
Fitting the Repeated Measures Model
The Error(Person/Time) term tells R that Time is nested within Person — each person contributes one score at each time point.
fit.ws <- aov(BP ~ Time + Error(Person/Time), data = mind.melt)
summary(fit.ws)
Error: Person
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
Residuals  9  11632    1292

Error: Person:Time
          Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)
Time       3  569.1   189.7   24.48 7.3e-08 ***
Residuals 27  209.2     7.8
Time has a statistically significant effect on blood pressure, F(3, 27) = 24.48, p < .001.






Note



Reading the output
The ANOVA table is split into two error strata. The Person stratum captures between-person variability (individual differences in average BP). The Person:Time stratum is where the test lives: it compares variance attributable to Time against the Person × Time interaction (the within-person error). Because individual differences are absorbed into the Person stratum rather than the error term, the test is more powerful than a between-subjects design would be.

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
section: Overall Effect Size: Partial Eta Squared
text:
Overall Effect Size: Partial Eta Squared
eta_squared(fit.ws)
# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)

Group       | Parameter | Eta2 (partial) |       95% CI
-------------------------------------------------------
Person:Time |      Time |           0.73 | [0.56, 1.00]
Partial η² = .73 — time accounts for 73% of the within-person variance in blood pressure. By Cohen’s conventions (small ≈ .01, medium ≈ .06, large ≈ .14), this is a very large effect.






Note



Partial eta squared in repeated measures
eta_squared() returns partial η² for repeated measures models, because it partitions variance relative to the within-person error (Person:Time) rather than total variance. This is the standard convention for within-subjects effects.

title: Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
text:
Post-hoc Tests: Tukey’s HSD
A significant omnibus F tells us that BP changed over time, but not when the changes occurred. We use Tukey’s HSD via emmeans to make all pairwise comparisons.
emm <- emmeans(fit.ws, ~ Time)
pairs(emm, adjust = "tukey")

 Before - SixMonth         10.0 1.24 27   8.034  <.0001

 OneMonth - SixMonth        7.1 1.24 27   5.704  <.0001
 ThreeMonth - SixMonth      3.4 1.24 27   2.731  0.0506

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates
BP did not significantly change from Before to One Month (p = .116), but all comparisons involving Three Month or Six Month against an earlier time point were significant or near-significant. By Six Months, BP had dropped 10 points from baseline (p < .001).

text:
Pairwise Effect Sizes: Cohen’s d
cohens_d() with paired = TRUE computes the standardized mean difference using the standard deviation of the difference scores.
cohens_d(mind$Before, mind$OneMonth,    paired = TRUE)
cohens_d(mind$Before, mind$ThreeMonth,  paired = TRUE)
cohens_d(mind$Before, mind$SixMonth,    paired = TRUE)
Before vs. One Month:

    Standardizing scores, finding areas under the normal curve, constructing confidence intervals, and writing your first R function.

title: Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
text:
The airquality Dataset
We will use R’s built-in airquality dataset throughout this script. It contains daily air quality measurements recorded in New York from May to September 1973.
# Preview the first 6 rows
head(airquality)
  Ozone Solar.R Wind Temp Month Day
1    41     190  7.4   67     5   1
2    36     118  8.0   72     5   2
3    12     149 12.6   74     5   3
4    18     313 11.5   62     5   4
5    NA      NA 14.3   56     5   5
6    28      NA 14.9   66     5   6
# Variable names
names(airquality)
[1] "Ozone"   "Solar.R" "Wind"    "Temp"    "Month"   "Day"
# Quick summary of all variables
summary(airquality)
Notice that Ozone and Solar.R contain NA values — this is missing data. R will return NA for any calculation that includes missing values unless you tell it to skip them.
mean(airquality$Ozone)           # returns NA because of missing values
mean(airquality$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE)   # na.rm = TRUE removes NAs before computing
[1] NA
[1] 42.12931






Tipna.rm = TRUE



Most base R summary functions (mean(), sd(), median()) accept na.rm = TRUE. Make it a habit when working with real data — missing values are the rule, not the exception.

title: Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
text:
Calculating Z-Scores
A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value falls above or below the mean. The formula is:
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\]
where \(x\) is the individual value, \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean, and \(s\) is the sample standard deviation.
Let’s compute the z-score for the Ozone reading in the first row of airquality (41 ppb).
ozone_value <- airquality$Ozone[1]        # select the first row
ozone_mean  <- mean(airquality$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE)
ozone_sd    <- sd(airquality$Ozone,   na.rm = TRUE)

z_score <- (ozone_value - ozone_mean) / ozone_sd
z_score
[1] -0.03423409
The first ozone reading is 0.034 standard deviations below the mean — very close to average.






NoteInterpreting a z-score










z-score
Interpretation




0
Exactly at the mean


+1
One SD above the mean (~84th percentile)


−1
One SD below the mean (~16th percentile)


+2 / −2
Two SDs from the mean — unusual (~5% of values fall this far or farther)


> ±3
Rare — flagged as a potential outlier

title: Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
text:
Automating Z-Scores with scale()
Writing the formula by hand works for a single value, but scale() standardizes an entire column at once.
ozone_z <- scale(airquality$Ozone)
head(ozone_z)
            [,1]
[1,] -0.03423409
[2,] -0.18580489
[3,] -0.91334473
[4,] -0.73145977
[5,]          NA
[6,] -0.42831817
scale() returns the same z-score as the manual calculation for the first row. Rows with NA in the original column remain NA in the output.






TipVerify for yourself



Compare the first value in ozone_z with the z_score you computed manually — they should match. This is a good habit: always verify that a convenience function gives the same result as your hand calculation before trusting it.

title: Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
text:
Area Under the Normal Curve
Once you have a z-score, you can find the probability of observing a value at least that extreme using pnorm().
pnorm(q, mean, sd) returns the cumulative probability — the area under the normal curve to the left of the value q.
# Probability of a score LESS than 350
# in a distribution with mean = 300, sd = 25
pnorm(350, 300, 25)
[1] 0.9772499
About 97.7% of scores fall below 350.
# Probability of a score GREATER than 350
# lower.tail = FALSE flips to the right-hand tail
pnorm(350, 300, 25, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 0.02275013
About 2.3% of scores exceed 350.






Notelower.tail = FALSE



By default, pnorm() gives you the left-tail area (P(X ≤ q)). Setting lower.tail = FALSE gives you the right-tail area (P(X > q)). These two always sum to 1.
Use lower.tail = FALSE when your research question asks “how likely is a score this high or higher?”

title: Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
text:
Confidence Intervals
A confidence interval (CI) gives a plausible range of values for the true population mean, based on sample data. A 95% CI, for example, means: if we repeated this study many times, 95% of the intervals we construct would contain the true population mean.
The formula for a z-based CI is:
\[\bar{x} \pm z^* \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where \(z^*\) is the critical value (from the standard normal distribution) corresponding to the desired confidence level.
We will use data from a satisfaction with life study: \(\bar{x} = 27\), \(s = 6.43\), \(n = 176\).
mean.life <- 27
sd.life   <- 6.43
n         <- 176






NoteWhy divide alpha by 2?



For a 95% CI, we want to capture the middle 95% of the distribution, leaving 5% in the tails. Because the normal distribution is symmetric, we split that 5% equally: 2.5% in each tail. So we find the z-score that cuts off the top 2.5% — that is, qnorm(0.025, lower.tail = FALSE), which equals 1.96.
In general: alpha = 1 − confidence level, and we use alpha / 2 for each tail.



80% Confidence Interval
Alpha = 1 − .80 = .20 → alpha/2 = .10
error80 <- qnorm(0.10, lower.tail = FALSE) * sd.life / sqrt(n)

lower80 <- mean.life - error80
upper80 <- mean.life + error80

lower80
upper80
[1] 26.37886
[1] 27.62114


90% Confidence Interval
Alpha = 1 − .90 = .10 → alpha/2 = .05
error90 <- qnorm(0.05, lower.tail = FALSE) * sd.life / sqrt(n)

lower90 <- mean.life - error90
upper90 <- mean.life + error90

lower90
upper90
[1] 26.20277
[1] 27.79723


95% Confidence Interval
Alpha = 1 − .95 = .05 → alpha/2 = .025
error95 <- qnorm(0.025, lower.tail = FALSE) * sd.life / sqrt(n)

lower95 <- mean.life - error95
upper95 <- mean.life + error95

lower95
upper95
[1] 26.05005
[1] 27.94995


99% Confidence Interval
Alpha = 1 − .99 = .01 → alpha/2 = .005
error99 <- qnorm(0.005, lower.tail = FALSE) * sd.life / sqrt(n)

lower99 <- mean.life - error99
upper99 <- mean.life + error99

lower99
upper99
[1] 25.75155
[1] 28.24845






TipWhat changes as confidence increases?



Notice that wider confidence levels produce wider intervals: the 99% CI is noticeably wider than the 80% CI. There is a trade-off — more confidence requires a wider net. A very wide interval is statistically safe but not very informative. In practice, 95% is the standard in psychology.

title: Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
section: The Z-Test: Writing Your First R Function
text:
The Z-Test: Writing Your First R Function
A z-test asks: given our sample mean, is the population mean plausibly equal to some hypothesized value \(\mu_0\)? The test statistic is:
\[z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\]
where \(\sigma\) is the known population standard deviation (unlike the t-test, which estimates \(\sigma\) from the sample).
R does not have a built-in z-test function, so we will write one. This is a good introduction to how functions work in R.
z.test <- function(x, mu, popdev) {

  # Step 1: Calculate the z-score and round to 3 decimal places
  z.score <- round((mean(x) - mu) / (popdev / sqrt(length(x))), 3)

  # Step 2: Find the one-tailed probability
  # pnorm(abs(z.score), lower.tail = FALSE) gives the area in the upper tail
  one.tail.p <- round(pnorm(abs(z.score), lower.tail = FALSE), 3)

  # Step 3: Print the results
  cat("z =", z.score, "\n",
      "one-tailed probability =", one.tail.p, "\n",
      "two-tailed probability =", 2 * one.tail.p)
}
The function takes three arguments:



Argument
Meaning




x
A vector of sample scores


mu
The hypothesized population mean (H₀)


popdev
The known population standard deviation



Now let’s test the function using a phonics study dataset. We have 10 scores and want to test whether the population mean could be 72, given a known population SD of 8.
phonics.data <- c(75.12, 73.82, 74.65, 75.33, 75.01,
                  74.27, 74.91, 74.63, 73.94, 75.08)

z.test(phonics.data, mu = 72, popdev = 8)
z = 1.058
 one-tailed probability = 0.145
 two-tailed probability = 0.29






NoteInterpreting the output



The sample mean is 74.676. The z-score of 1.058 tells us the sample mean is about 1 standard error above the hypothesized mean of 72. The two-tailed p-value of .29 is well above the conventional alpha of .05, so we fail to reject H₀ — the data do not provide sufficient evidence that the population mean differs from 72.
The function uses abs(z.score) when computing the probability so that the one-tailed result is always the upper-tail area — this works correctly regardless of whether the z-score is positive or negative.

title: All About t-Tests
text:
Checking Assumptions
Before running a t-test, check two key assumptions: normality of the data within each group, and homogeneity of variance (equal spreads) between groups.

Shapiro-Wilk Test of Normality
The Shapiro-Wilk test assesses whether a variable is plausibly drawn from a normal distribution.

H₀: The data are normally distributed
H₁: The data are not normally distributed

A non-significant result (p > .05) means we fail to reject normality — the data are consistent with a normal distribution. Subset by group before testing:
## Test normality within each group
shapiro.test(scores$scores[scores$intervention == 1])
shapiro.test(scores$scores[scores$intervention == 2])
    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  scores$scores[scores$intervention == 1]
W = 0.98198, p-value = 0.8101


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  scores$scores[scores$intervention == 2]
W = 0.9688, p-value = 0.3937
Both groups pass the normality test: W values close to 1 and p-values well above .05 indicate no evidence of departure from normality. We can proceed with confidence.






NoteWhen normality is violated



If the Shapiro-Wilk test is significant (p < .05), the t-test is still reasonably robust with large samples (n ≥ 30 per group). For small samples with clear non-normality, consider a non-parametric alternative such as the Mann-Whitney U test (wilcox.test()).

title: All About t-Tests
text:
One-Sample t-Test
A one-sample t-test asks whether a sample mean is significantly different from a known or hypothesized population mean (\(\mu_0\)). The test statistic is:
\[t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\]
The key difference from the z-test is that we use the sample standard deviation \(s\) instead of a known population \(\sigma\). This introduces more uncertainty, which is accounted for by the t-distribution (discussed further at the end of this script).

One-Tailed Test
A one-tailed test has a directional alternative hypothesis: we predict the mean is either greater than or less than \(\mu_0\).
Is the sample mean significantly higher than a national average reading score of 150?
## H0: mean = 150
## H1: mean > 150  (one-tailed, upper)
t.test(scores$scores, mu = 150, alternative = "greater")
    One Sample t-test

data:  scores$scores
t = 16.41, df = 71, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean is greater than 150
95 percent confidence interval:
 180.9963      Inf
sample estimates:
mean of x
    184.5
The t-statistic of 16.41 is far into the upper tail, and the p-value is essentially zero. We reject H₀ and conclude that the sample mean (184.5) is significantly higher than 150.


Two-Tailed Test
A two-tailed test has a non-directional alternative: we only predict that the mean is different from \(\mu_0\).
## H0: mean = 150
## H1: mean ≠ 150  (two-tailed)
t.test(scores$scores, mu = 150, alternative = "two.sided")
    One Sample t-test

data:  scores$scores
t = 16.41, df = 71, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 150
95 percent confidence interval:
 180.3081 188.6919
sample estimates:
mean of x
    184.5
The t-statistic is the same (16.41) — only the CI and p-value calculation differ. The 95% CI [180.31, 188.69] does not include 150, confirming the result.






NoteOne-tailed vs. two-tailed: which to use?



Use a two-tailed test unless you have a strong, pre-registered directional prediction. Two-tailed tests are more conservative and are the default in most psychological research. Switching to one-tailed after seeing your data inflates Type I error.

title: All About t-Tests
text:
Two-Sample t-Test (Independent Samples)
A two-sample independent t-test compares the means of two separate, unrelated groups. We look at the sampling distribution of the difference between means.
There are two versions depending on whether we assume the two groups have equal population variances.

Equal Variances Assumed
## H0: mean(group 1) = mean(group 2)
## H1: means are not equal
t.test(scores$scores ~ scores$intervention, var.equal = TRUE)
    Two Sample t-test

data:  scores$scores by scores$intervention
t = 4.5757, df = 70, p-value = 2e-05
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 1 and group 2 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  9.590143 24.409857
sample estimates:
mean in group 1 mean in group 2
            193             176


Unequal Variances (Welch’s t-Test)
## Welch correction: does not assume equal variances
t.test(scores$scores ~ scores$intervention, var.equal = FALSE)
    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  scores$scores by scores$intervention
t = 4.5757, df = 66.636, p-value = 2.125e-05
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 1 and group 2 is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  9.58356 24.41644
sample estimates:
mean in group 1 mean in group 2
            193             176






NoteEqual vs. unequal variances: Welch’s correction



When variances are unequal, the Welch version adjusts the degrees of freedom downward (here, from 70 to 66.636) to compensate for the additional uncertainty. The t-statistic stays the same, but the p-value changes slightly.
In practice: Welch’s t-test (var.equal = FALSE) is recommended as the default. It performs just as well as the equal-variance test when variances are equal, and it is more accurate when they are not. Always run Levene’s test first (see below) to check the assumption.

title: All About t-Tests
text:
Paired Samples t-Test
A paired t-test is used when the same participants (or matched pairs) provide scores under two conditions. Instead of comparing two independent groups, we compute the difference score for each participant and test whether the mean difference is zero.
The formula is the same as the one-sample t-test, applied to the difference scores:
\[t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}\]
Here we use data from the mindfulness stress study on the slides. Stress was measured before and after one month of mindfulness practice for 10 participants.
before <- c(195, 198, 201, 187, 205, 155, 187, 190, 234, 187)
after  <- c(194, 190, 200, 200, 152, 185, 190, 220, 180, 180)

## H0: mean difference = 0
## H1: stress is higher before than after (one-tailed: before > after)
t.test(before, after, alternative = "greater", paired = TRUE)
    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 0.52277, df = 9, p-value = 0.3069
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is greater than 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -12.0314      Inf
sample estimates:
mean difference
            4.8
The mean stress score dropped by 4.8 points on average, but this difference is not statistically significant (t = 0.52, p = .31). With only 10 participants and substantial variability in stress change across individuals, we do not have enough evidence to conclude that mindfulness reduced stress.

title: All About t-Tests
text:
Effect Sizes
Statistical significance tells you whether an effect is real — but not how big it is. Effect sizes are standardized measures that express the magnitude of a difference in units that can be compared across studies.

Cohen’s d (Independent Samples)
Cohen’s d divides the mean difference by the pooled standard deviation:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_\text{pooled}}\]
Conventional benchmarks: small = 0.2, medium = 0.5, large = 0.8.
## install.packages("effectsize")
library(effectsize)

cohens_d(scores$scores ~ scores$intervention)
Cohen's d |       95% CI
------------------------
1.08      | [0.58, 1.57]

- Estimated using pooled SD.
d = 1.08 is a large effect — the two interventions differ by more than one full standard deviation. Despite the non-significant Levene test (variances are fairly similar), the practical difference between groups is substantial.


Cohen’s d (Paired Samples)
For paired data, Cohen’s d uses the standard deviation of the difference scores:
\[d = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d}\]
You can also compute it manually before passing it to cohens_d():
before <- c(195, 198, 201, 187, 205, 155, 187, 190, 234, 187)
after  <- c(194, 190, 200, 200, 152, 185, 190, 220, 180, 180)

## Manual calculation
m_D  <- mean(before - after)   # mean difference
sd_D <- sd(before - after)     # SD of differences

m_D                   # 4.8
sd_D                  # 29.04
m_D / sd_D            # Cohen's d = 0.165

## Or let the package do it
cohens_d(before, after, paired = TRUE)
[1] 4.8
[1] 29.03561
[1] 0.1653142

Cohen's d |        95% CI
-------------------------
0.17      | [-0.46, 0.79]
d = 0.17 is a small effect and the CI crosses zero, consistent with the non-significant t-test result.


Hedges’ g (Corrected for Small Samples)
For small samples (n < 20), Hedges’ g applies a correction factor that shrinks Cohen’s d slightly downward to reduce bias:
hedges_g(before, after, paired = TRUE)
Hedges' g |        95% CI
-------------------------
0.15      | [-0.42, 0.72]






NoteCohen’s d vs. Hedges’ g



Both measure effect size, but Hedges’ g is preferred when your sample is small (roughly n < 20). The correction is small but matters: here d = 0.17 shrinks to g = 0.15. With larger samples the two converge. When in doubt, report Hedges’ g — it is the more conservative and unbiased estimate.

title: All About t-Tests
section: Levene’s Test: Can We Assume Equal Variances?
text:
Levene’s Test: Can We Assume Equal Variances?
Before choosing between the equal-variance and Welch versions of the independent t-test, check whether the two groups have similar variance using Levene’s test.

H₀: The variances are equal (homogeneity of variance holds)
H₁: The variances are not equal

A significant result means the equal-variance assumption is violated — use Welch’s t-test.
## Install lawstat once if you haven't already:
## install.packages("lawstat")
library(lawstat)

levene.test(scores$scores, group = scores$intervention)
    Modified robust Brown-Forsythe Levene-type test based on the absolute
    deviations from the median

data:  scores$scores
Test Statistic = 1.1056, p-value = 0.2966






TipReading the Levene output



Look at the p-value. If p > .05, you fail to reject H₀ and may proceed with the equal-variance t-test. If p < .05, variances differ significantly — use Welch’s (var.equal = FALSE).
Here p = .297 — well above .05. The variances are not significantly different, so the equal-variance assumption holds. That said, Welch’s t-test (var.equal = FALSE) is always a safe default because it performs equally well when variances are equal and is more accurate when they are not.

Visualizing the Results

A box plot shows the median, interquartile range, and any outliers for each group.

Bar graphs with error bars (showing ± 1 standard error) are standard for reporting group means in psychology.

Each error bar extends ±1 standard error above and below the bar. When error bars from two groups do not overlap, this is a visual signal (though not a formal test) that the group means may differ significantly.

section: t-Critical Values and the Link to z
text:
t-Critical Values and the Link to z
Use qt() to find the t-critical value for any combination of alpha and degrees of freedom — the value your t-statistic must exceed to reach significance.
## qt(p, df, lower.tail = FALSE)
## p = alpha/2 for a two-tailed test (0.025 at alpha = .05)
## df = degrees of freedom

qt(0.025,    5, lower.tail = FALSE)
qt(0.025,   10, lower.tail = FALSE)
qt(0.025,   25, lower.tail = FALSE)
qt(0.025,   30, lower.tail = FALSE)
qt(0.025,  100, lower.tail = FALSE)
qt(0.025, 1000, lower.tail = FALSE)

NoteAs df increases, t approaches z



Notice the pattern: as degrees of freedom grow, the t-critical value falls toward 1.96 — the familiar z-critical value for a two-tailed test at α = .05.

This is not a coincidence. The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution to account for the extra uncertainty introduced by estimating the population SD from a small sample. As n (and therefore df) increases, that estimate becomes more precise and the t-distribution gradually narrows until it is indistinguishable from z.
You can verify this with qnorm():


## The z-critical value (equivalent to t with infinite df)
qnorm(0.025, lower.tail = FALSE)
[1] 1.959964
With 1000 degrees of freedom the t-critical value (1.962) is already within 0.002 of the z-critical value (1.960). By the time you have a few hundred participants, the practical difference between a t-test and a z-test is negligible — the reason we use t is that for small samples, those extra decimal points matter.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA

PSY 771 · ANOVA and Experimental Design
    
    Verifying the statistical assumptions that underlie ANOVA — and what to do when they are violated.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA
text:
Overview
ANOVA models rest on a set of statistical assumptions. When these assumptions hold, the F test behaves as expected. When they are violated, p-values and confidence intervals may be misleading. This script walks through how to check each assumption in R and how to respond when a violation is detected.
We will work with the mind2 dataset — a mindfulness program study that tracked blood pressure (BP) in 10 participants across four time points: Before, One Month, Three Months, and Six Months.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA
text:
The Assumptions
Three assumptions apply to all ANOVA designs (one-way, two-way between-subjects, and repeated-measures):

Independence of observations — scores from different people must not influence one another
Homogeneity of variance (homoscedasticity) — the variance of the residuals should be roughly equal across groups or conditions
Normality — the residuals (or population scores) should be approximately normally distributed

Repeated-measures ANOVA adds a fourth:

Sphericity — the variances of the difference scores between all pairs of conditions must be equal

We test these using residuals from the fitted model. We start by fitting the model using lme() from the nlme package, which makes it easy to extract residuals from a repeated-measures design.

fit_lme <- lme(BP ~ Time, random = ~1|Person, data = mind2)
anova(fit_lme)

            numDF denDF  F-value p-value
(Intercept)     1    27 344.6427  <.0001
Time            3    27  24.4851  <.0001


The model confirms what Script 6 showed: there is a significant effect of time, F(3, 27) = 24.49, p < .001. Now we check whether the assumptions of this model are satisfied.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA
text:
Assumption 1: Independence

model.res    <- residuals(fit_lme)
model.fitted <- fitted(fit_lme)

plot(model.res,
     ylab = "Residuals",
     xlab = "Observation Index",
     main = "Residuals by Observation Order")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")














Note



In a repeated-measures design, the residuals will not look completely random. Because the same person contributes multiple observations, there is built-in correlation — and that is expected. If the residuals looked perfectly independent and scattered, it would actually suggest the within-subject correlation is not being captured by the model. What you are looking for is the absence of systematic drift or clustering across the plot.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA
text:
Assumption 2: Homogeneity of Variance (Homoscedasticity)
A residuals vs. fitted values plot is the standard diagnostic for homoscedasticity. If the assumption holds, the spread of residuals should be roughly consistent across the range of fitted values — a horizontal band with no fanning or narrowing.

plot(model.fitted, model.res,
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")








In this plot, the spread of the residuals appears to change across fitted values, which suggests unequal variance. This is not unusual in repeated-measures data, but it should be addressed.

Formal Test: Likelihood Ratio Test
We can formally test whether allowing condition-specific residual variances improves the model fit. We fit a second model that explicitly allows each time point to have its own residual variance, then compare the two models using a likelihood ratio test.

fit_lme_unequal <- lme(
  BP ~ Time,
  random  = ~1|Person,
  data    = mind2,
  weights = varIdent(form = ~1|Time)
)

anova(fit_lme, fit_lme_unequal)

                Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value
fit_lme             1  6 243.1303 252.6315 -115.5652                        
fit_lme_unequal     2  9 229.7751 244.0268 -105.8876 1 vs 2 19.35524   2e-04


The likelihood ratio test shows a significant improvement when allowing unequal variances across time points, χ²(3) = 19.36, p < .001. The model with unequal variances also has lower AIC (229.78 vs. 243.13) and lower BIC (244.03 vs. 252.63).






Tip



Lower AIC and BIC indicate a better-fitting model. Both criteria favor the heterogeneous-variance model here, confirming that the equal-variance assumption is violated. For final reporting, results should be based on fit_lme_unequal rather than the original model.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA
text:
Assumption 3: Normality
A Q-Q (quantile–quantile) plot compares the distribution of the residuals to what we would expect if they came from a normal distribution. Points that fall closely along the diagonal line indicate approximate normality.

qqnorm(model.res, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
qqline(model.res, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)








In this plot, several departures from normality are visible:

Heavy tails at both ends: points deviate from the line at the extremes
Lower tail deviation: the most pronounced departure is in the lower tail (around −2 theoretical quantiles), where points fall below the line
S-shaped pattern: suggests possible skewness in the distribution

These patterns indicate that the residuals have heavier tails than a normal distribution and may be slightly negatively skewed. With only 10 participants, the Q-Q plot has limited resolution, and ANOVA is reasonably robust to mild normality violations when sample sizes are equal across conditions.

title: PSY 771 — Script 8: Assumption Testing in ANOVA
text:
Assumption 4: Sphericity (Repeated-Measures Only)
Sphericity requires that the variances of the difference scores between all pairs of time points are equal. For example, the variance of (Before − OneMonth) should equal the variance of (Before − SixMonth) and the variance of (OneMonth − SixMonth), and so on.
If sphericity is violated, the F test from a standard repeated-measures ANOVA is too liberal — it rejects the null hypothesis more often than it should.






Note



The aov() function used in Script 6 does not test sphericity or apply corrections for it. To test and correct for sphericity violations, we use the Anova() function from the car package.



Restructuring the Data
The Anova() function from car requires the data in wide format — one row per participant, one column per time point.

shortmind <- with(mind2, cbind(
  BP[Time == "Before"],
  BP[Time == "OneMonth"],
  BP[Time == "ThreeMonth"],
  BP[Time == "SixMonth"]
))

mind.model <- lm(shortmind ~ 1)
TimePoint  <- factor(1:4)



Running the Test

fit_sph <- Anova(mind.model,
                 idata   = data.frame(TimePoint),
                 idesign = ~TimePoint,
                 type    = "III")

summary(fit_sph, multivariate = FALSE)


Univariate Type III Repeated-Measures ANOVA Assuming Sphericity

            Sum Sq num Df Error SS den Df F value    Pr(>F)    
(Intercept) 445421      1  11631.7      9 344.643 1.749e-08 ***
TimePoint      569      3    209.2     27  24.485 7.305e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Mauchly Tests for Sphericity

          Test statistic    p-value
TimePoint      0.0098901 1.4697e-06


Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt Corrections
 for Departure from Sphericity

           GG eps Pr(>F[GG])    
TimePoint 0.38075  0.0004042 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

             HF eps   Pr(>F[HF])
TimePoint 0.3997112 0.0003089785




Reading the Output
The output has three parts:
Univariate Type III Repeated-Measures ANOVA Assuming Sphericity This is the standard F test, computed under the assumption that sphericity holds. Use these values only if the Mauchly test is non-significant.
Mauchly Tests for Sphericity The null hypothesis is that sphericity holds. We want p > .05 to retain the assumption. Here, p < .001, which means sphericity is violated. We should not rely on the uncorrected F test.
Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt Corrections When sphericity is violated, these corrections adjust the degrees of freedom to produce a more conservative F test. Both corrections still yield p < .001, so the main effect of time remains significant even after accounting for the sphericity violation.






Tip



Which correction to report? The Greenhouse-Geisser (GG) correction is more conservative and is generally preferred when the GG epsilon (ε) is below 0.75. Here, GG ε = 0.38, so report the Greenhouse-Geisser corrected values.

title: Research
text:
LETR Lab
    Research
    We explore the processes underlying learning across contexts and for all learners — examining individual differences in cognition, language, and motivation.
  




  Current Focus
  New Projects
  Two new projects launching in the coming year bring eye-tracking and multimodal AI into the lab's research program.

  

    
      👁️
      Patricia Miller Fund
      Profiling Readers with Eye Tracking
      
        Readers differ meaningfully in the cognitive, motivational, and knowledge-based resources they bring to a text — yet prior research on reader profiles has relied almost entirely on self-report and performance measures, leaving eye movement data largely absent. This project integrates gaze behavior into a person-centered investigation of reading comprehension, comparing neurotypical readers and readers on the autism spectrum. Using the Microsoft HoloLens with VeYezer Graph eye tracking software, participants can move freely during reading — overcoming a key limitation of traditional static trackers that are especially burdensome for individuals with ASD. The study examines fixations, regressions, span of recognition, and fixation duration alongside background knowledge, prior interest, and engagement, asking whether existing reader profiles hold, require refinement, or differ across populations.
      
    

    
      🤝
      Ken Fong Translational Research Award
      Vision[AI]ry: Emotion & Attention Analytics for Education
      
        Students' emotional states directly shape learning — yet instructors in online environments lack the moment-to-moment visibility needed to detect confusion, frustration, or disengagement. In collaboration with Dr. Sanchita Ghose (Computer Engineering, AI-LAMP Lab), this project develops Vision[AI]ry, a multimodal platform that fuses facial expression analysis, vocal emotion recognition, and gaze-based attention tracking into real-time engagement scores. The system integrates three components — facial landmark detection via CNN, audio Mel-spectrogram analysis, and posture-based attention tracking — through a novel multimodal fusion algorithm deployed on edge computing hardware with low latency. The psychological component focuses on validating Vision[AI]ry against established self-report measures of learning-relevant affect (confusion, frustration, boredom, engaged concentration), with classroom deployment planned in online psychology and engineering courses. The platform will be released as open-source software for educational institutions.
      
    

  

  

  Ongoing Work
  Other Research Areas
  Alongside the new projects, the lab continues work in three areas developed over the past several years.

  

    
      📖
      Reading Across Mediums

text:
PSY 771 · ANOVA and Experimental Design
    R Scripts
    R code files for all topics covered in the course. New scripts will be added each week.
  




  Course Scripts
  Getting Started
  Work through these two scripts before the first class session.

  
    Script 1

    
      Introduction to R
      What R is, how to install it, and the core building blocks — arithmetic, objects, vectors, matrices, and data frames. Start here if you are new to R.
    

  

  
    Script 2

    
      Descriptives, Correlation & Regression
      A complete data analysis workflow: importing a real psychology dataset, computing descriptive statistics with psych::describe(), testing correlations with cor.test(), and fitting a multiple regression with lm().
    

  

  
    Script 3

    
      Z-Scores, Confidence Intervals, and the Z-Test
      Standardizing scores with the z-score formula and scale(), finding areas under the normal curve with pnorm(), constructing 80/90/95/99% confidence intervals with qnorm(), and writing a custom z.test() function in R.
    

  

  
    Script 4

    
      All About t-Tests
      One-sample, independent samples (equal and Welch), and paired t-tests using a reading intervention dataset. Includes Levene's test for homogeneity of variance, bar graphs with error bars, and a demonstration of how the t-distribution converges to z as sample size increases.
    

  

  
    Script 5

    
      One-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA
      Testing whether reading time differs across device types (phone, tablet, laptop). Covers assumption checking (Shapiro-Wilk, Levene's test), fitting the model with lm() and aov(), eta squared as an overall effect size, and post-hoc comparisons with Tukey's HSD and Cohen's d.
    

  

  
    Script 6

    
      Repeated Measures (Within-Subjects) ANOVA
      Testing whether blood pressure changes across four time points (Before, One Month, Three Months, Six Months) using the same participants. Covers the between-subjects vs. within-subjects distinction, reshaping data from wide to long format with melt(), assumption checking (normality of difference scores, sphericity), fitting the model with aov() and an Error() term, partial eta squared, Tukey's HSD via emmeans, confidence intervals, and Cohen's d for pairwise comparisons.
    

  

  
    Script 7

    
      Two-Factor Between-Subjects ANOVA
      Testing the effects of device type (Phone, Tablet, Laptop) and lighting condition (Blue, White, Yellow, Natural) on reading time in a 3 × 4 factorial design. Covers recoding factor levels with factor(), interaction plots, fitting the model with a Device * Light term, interpreting the ANOVA table (main effects and interaction), partial eta squared, and how a non-significant interaction guides the decision to interpret main effects directly. Post-hoc section uses Tukey's HSD via emmeans with confidence intervals and Cohen's d for pairwise comparisons of both factors.
    

  

  
    Script 8

    
      Assumption Testing in ANOVA
      Verifying the four assumptions that underlie ANOVA — independence, homoscedasticity, normality, and (for repeated-measures designs) sphericity. Covers residual diagnostic plots, likelihood ratio tests for unequal variance using lme() from the nlme package, Q-Q plots, and Mauchly's test with Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt corrections via the car package.
    

  

  
    Script 9

    
      Mixed Factorial ANOVA
      Analyzing designs that combine a between-subjects factor (reading medium: book vs. e-book) and a within-subjects factor (text genre: narrative, expository, mixed) in a single model. Covers the Error(subjects/genre) term in aov(), generalized eta squared, and simple effects analysis — examining genre differences within each medium (using aov() with error terms) and medium differences within each genre (using lm()).

text: The dataset for this week is readtime.csv. We will use this data to determine if reading time (in milliseconds) differs by type of device (1 = phone, 2 = tablet, 3 = laptop).

title: One-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Checking Assumptions

Normality
One-way ANOVA assumes that the residuals are normally distributed. We test this with a Shapiro-Wilk test on the model residuals (after fitting the model below) rather than on raw scores within each group.
fit2 <- aov(ReadingTime ~ Device, data = reader)
shapiro.test(fit2$residuals)
    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  fit2$residuals
W = 0.98523, p-value = 0.6822
The test is non-significant (p = .682), so we have no evidence against normality.


Homogeneity of Variance
ANOVA assumes equal variances across groups (homoscedasticity). We test this with Levene’s test.
levene.test(reader$ReadingTime, reader$Device)
    Modified robust Brown-Forsythe Levene-type test based on the
    absolute deviations from the median

data:  reader$ReadingTime
Test Statistic = 0.061395, p-value = 0.9405
The test is non-significant (p = .941), confirming equal variances. The standard ANOVA is appropriate.






Note



If Levene’s test is significant, use a Welch one-way ANOVA instead: oneway.test(ReadingTime ~ Device, data = reader, var.equal = FALSE) This does not assume equal variances, analogous to Welch’s correction for the independent-samples t-test.

title: One-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Overall Effect Size: Eta Squared
Before drilling into which pairs differ, quantify the overall effect of device type. Eta squared (η²) is the proportion of total variance in reading time explained by device.
eta_squared(fit1, partial = FALSE)
# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)

Parameter | Eta2 |       95% CI
-------------------------------
Device    | 0.12 | [0.01, 1.00]
η² = .12 — device type explains about 12% of the variance in reading time, a medium effect by Cohen’s conventions (small ≈ .01, medium ≈ .06, large ≈ .14).






Note



η² vs. partial η²: In a one-way design these are identical. In factorial designs (Week 10+) they diverge — partial η² measures the effect of one factor after removing the other factors, so values from different studies are not directly comparable. Always report which you computed.

title: One-Way Between-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Post-hoc Tests
A significant ANOVA tells us that at least one group mean differs — but not which ones. Post-hoc tests make all pairwise comparisons while controlling the familywise Type I error rate.


Tukey’s HSD (Recommended)
Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference uses the studentized range distribution to test all pairwise comparisons simultaneously. It is designed specifically for this purpose and is the standard recommendation for balanced or near-balanced designs.
TukeyHSD(fit2)
  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

$Device
         diff       lwr        upr     p adj
2-1 -220.6260 -449.4258   8.173844 0.0610
3-1 -238.8265 -467.6263 -10.026656 0.0389 *
3-2  -18.2005 -247.0003 210.599344 0.9800
Laptop users read significantly faster than phone users (mean difference = −238.83 ms, p = .039). The tablet vs. phone comparison approached but did not reach significance (p = .061). Tablet and laptop did not differ (p = .980).


Confidence Intervals for Tukey Pairwise Differences
TukeyHSD() already includes confidence intervals in its output. We can also obtain them using the emmeans workflow, which integrates cleanly with pairwise comparisons and effect size calculations.
em_fit <- emmeans(fit2, ~ Device)
tukey_results <- pairs(em_fit, adjust = "tukey")
confint(tukey_results, adjust = "tukey")
 contrast          estimate   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 Device1 - Device2    220.6 95.1 57    -8.17      449
 Device1 - Device3    238.8 95.1 57    10.03      468
 Device2 - Device3     18.2 95.1 57  -210.60      247

Confidence level used: 0.95
Conf-level adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates
The 95% CI for Device 1 − Device 3 [10.03, 468] does not include 0, confirming a significant difference. The CI for Device 1 − Device 2 [−8.17, 449] just crosses 0, consistent with the marginal p = .061.



Pairwise Effect Sizes: Cohen’s d
Statistical significance tells us whether groups differ; effect sizes tell us how much. Cohen’s d is a standardized mean difference. For post-hoc comparisons after ANOVA, we use the pooled error term from the model (rather than just the two groups’ SDs), which is more stable and consistent across comparisons.
d_results <- eff_size(emmeans(fit2, pairwise ~ Device),
                      sigma = sigma(fit2),
                      edf = df.residual(fit2),
                      ci = TRUE)
d_results
 contrast            effect.size    SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 (Device1 - Device2)      0.7338 0.324 57   0.0858    1.382
 (Device1 - Device3)      0.7943 0.325 57   0.1438    1.445
 (Device2 - Device3)      0.0605 0.316 57  -0.5728    0.694

sigma used for effect sizes: 300.7
Phone vs. tablet: d = 0.73 (medium-large); phone vs. laptop: d = 0.79 (large); tablet vs. laptop: d = 0.06 (negligible). The significant Tukey comparison (phone vs. laptop) corresponds to a large effect.



Bonferroni Correction






Warning



Planned vs. exploratory comparisons
There are two fundamentally different situations for multiple comparisons:

Planned (a priori) comparisons: You specified exact hypotheses before collecting data. For example, “I predict phone will differ from laptop.” In this case, Bonferroni is appropriate — you divide α by the number of tests you committed to in advance.
Exploratory (post-hoc) comparisons: You run all pairwise tests after finding a significant omnibus ANOVA, scanning for differences. This is the more common situation, and it is why we need stricter corrections. Bonferroni is overly conservative here — it was designed for a small set of independent tests, not the correlated structure of all-pairwise comparisons. Use Tukey’s HSD instead, which is purpose-built for this scenario and offers better power with the same familywise error control.



emmeans(fit2, pairwise ~ Device, adjust = "bonferroni")
$contrasts
 contrast          estimate   SE df t.ratio p.value
 Device1 - Device2    220.6 95.1 57   2.320  0.0718
 Device1 - Device3    238.8 95.1 57   2.512  0.0446
 Device2 - Device3     18.2 95.1 57   0.191  1.0000

P value adjustment: bonferroni method for 3 tests
The p-values shown are already adjusted — compare them to α = .05, not .0167. With Bonferroni, no comparison reaches significance. Compare this to Tukey’s HSD, which identified phone vs. laptop as significant (p = .039): Tukey is the more appropriate tool for exploratory post-hoc comparisons, and it has better power.
To get confidence intervals for the Bonferroni-adjusted comparisons:
bonf_results <- pairs(em_fit, adjust = "bonferroni")
confint(bonf_results, adjust = "bonferroni")
 contrast          estimate   SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 Device1 - Device2    220.6 95.1 57    -13.9      455
 Device1 - Device3    238.8 95.1 57      4.3      473
 Device2 - Device3     18.2 95.1 57   -216.3      253

Confidence level used: 0.95
Conf-level adjustment: bonferroni method for 3 estimates
Notice that the Bonferroni CI for Device 1 − Device 3 [4.3, 473] is slightly wider than the Tukey CI [10.03, 468], and its lower bound is closer to 0. This reflects the added conservatism of the Bonferroni correction — it requires a larger observed difference before excluding 0 from the interval.



Fisher’s LSD
Fisher’s LSD performs standard t-tests between all pairs using the pooled MSE. It appears frequently in older published literature but does not adequately control the familywise error rate when there are more than three groups. You may encounter it in papers, but Tukey’s HSD is preferred for new analyses.

title: PSY 771 — Script 9: Mixed Factorial ANOVA
text:
What Is a Mixed ANOVA?
A mixed factorial ANOVA — sometimes called a split-plot ANOVA — combines features of the two designs you have already seen:

A between-subjects factor: different participants appear in each level (like the two-way ANOVA in Script 7)
A within-subjects factor: the same participants appear at every level (like the repeated-measures ANOVA in Script 6)

The word “mixed” refers to the fact that the design is a mixture of these two structures — not to any mixing of data values.

title: PSY 771 — Script 9: Mixed Factorial ANOVA
text:
The Study
Researchers examined how reading medium (book vs. e-book) and text genre (narrative, expository, mixed) affect reading comprehension scores. Eight participants were randomly assigned to read either physical books (book) or e-readers (ebook). Each participant then read and was tested on all three genre types.



Factor
Type
Levels




Medium
Between-subjects
book, ebook


Genre
Within-subjects
narrative, expository, mixed



Because medium is between-subjects, the four book readers are entirely different people from the four ebook readers. Because genre is within-subjects, every participant was tested on all three genre types.

Interaction Plot

interaction.plot(mixed.data$genre, mixed.data$medium, mixed.data$score,
                 type = "b", lwd = 3, pch = c(16, 17), lty = 1,

The two lines are not parallel — the gap between book and ebook readers is much larger for some genre conditions than others. Book readers score noticeably lower on expository and mixed texts compared to ebook readers, but the two groups are more similar on narrative texts. This non-parallel pattern is the visual signature of an interaction.

title: PSY 771 — Script 9: Mixed Factorial ANOVA
text:
The Mixed ANOVA Model
The model formula includes both the main effects and their interaction. The Error() term is the key addition for mixed designs. It tells R about the two separate error strata:

subjects — the between-subjects error (variance among individuals assigned to different media)
subjects:genre — the within-subjects error (how much a person’s scores vary across genre conditions)


mixed.anova <- aov(score ~ medium * genre + Error(subjects/genre),
                   data = mixed.data)
summary(mixed.anova)


Error: subjects

medium     1  108.4  108.37   1.227   0.31
Residuals  6  529.9   88.32               

Error: subjects:genre

genre         2  40.08   20.04   5.681 0.018366 *  
medium:genre  2 120.25   60.13  17.043 0.000312 ***
Residuals    12  42.33    3.53                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1








Note



Reading the two error tables: The output shows two sections. The Error: subjects table tests the between-subjects effect (medium). The Error: subjects:genre table tests the within-subjects effects (genre and the medium × genre interaction). Each effect is tested against the appropriate error term for its design type.

The main effect of medium is not significant — book and ebook readers do not differ overall. The main effect of genre is significant — comprehension scores differ across text types on average. But both of these main effects are qualified by the significant medium × genre interaction, F(2, 12) = 17.04, p < .001. When an interaction is significant, the main effects cannot be interpreted in isolation. We need to examine the simple effects: how genre operates separately within each medium, and how medium operates separately within each genre.

title: PSY 771 — Script 9: Mixed Factorial ANOVA
text:
Effect Sizes: Generalized Eta Squared

eta_squared(mixed.anova, generalized = TRUE)

# Effect Size for ANOVA (Type I)

Group          |    Parameter | Eta2 (generalized) |       95% CI
-----------------------------------------------------------------
subjects       |       medium |               0.16 | [0.00, 1.00]
subjects:genre |        genre |               0.07 | [0.00, 1.00]
subjects:genre | medium:genre |               0.17 | [0.00, 1.00]

- Observed variables: All
- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].


For mixed designs, generalized eta squared (η²_G) is the preferred effect size. Unlike partial eta squared, it accounts for variability from all sources in the design and is comparable across studies that use different designs. Here, the interaction accounts for approximately 17% of the total variance in comprehension scores.

The pattern for ebook readers is essentially the reverse of the pattern for book readers — mixed texts led to the highest comprehension scores, and narrative texts were lowest.






Tip



This reversal in the direction of the genre effect across the two medium conditions is exactly what the significant interaction was telling us. Book readers comprehend narrative texts best; ebook readers comprehend mixed texts best. No single “best genre” exists when the interaction is present.

For mixed-genre texts, the medium difference is marginal, F(1, 6) = 4.78, p = .071, η²_G = .44. Ebook readers (M = 53.2) outperformed book readers (M = 45.0), and the confidence interval for the ebook–book difference includes zero (95% CI [−1.0, 17.5]), meaning the data are consistent with no difference — but also consistent with a difference as large as 17.5 points. The large effect size despite the non-significant p-value reflects the small sample size (4 per group).






Note



Why use lm() here instead of aov() with an Error() term? When we subset to a single genre level, there is no longer a within-subjects structure — each participant appears in only one row. This is a standard between-subjects comparison, so ordinary lm() is correct. The Error() term is only needed when the same participants appear across multiple rows of the same analysis.

title: PSY 771 — Script 9: Mixed Factorial ANOVA
text:
Summary
The mixed factorial ANOVA found a significant medium × genre interaction, F(2, 12) = 17.04, p < .001, η²_G = .17. The effect of genre on comprehension differed depending on reading medium:

Book readers comprehended narrative texts significantly better than expository or mixed texts
Ebook readers comprehended mixed texts best, with narrative texts producing the lowest scores among ebook readers

The main effect of medium was not significant overall, but the interaction reveals that ebook readers had an advantage specifically for expository and mixed texts, while book and ebook readers performed similarly on narrative texts.
